title: The Mystery of Christ and the New Life
english: …to the sanctified people, obviously through the Spirit, and purified through faith, he fiercely and bitterly attacked, and the Church of God was besieged by the most wicked phalanx of spirits under his hand.
Perhaps he thought he could turn it back, but he was foolish and did not understand anything, for it was not possible for him to capture the holy city of God, the heavenly Jerusalem.

For who can resist the all-powerful God? Therefore, the beast-like enemy has been destroyed along with his own attendants, and he has been driven away from the flock of the pious, as a wild beast leaps upon them.
The Savior taught us, saying: 'Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out. If I am lifted up on the earth, I will draw all to myself' (John 12:31-32).

For the passion of Christ was the overthrow of death, the destruction of the devil, and the abolition of sin, through his being lifted up on the cross and casting down the boast of the devil into the earth.

At the appointed time, God, who is the God of all, introduces the word concerning the birth of the Only-Begotten in the flesh, and reveals the mystery through the voice of prophets, so that having completed the events, he might receive faith from all.
He says: 'Behold, the Lord Sabaoth will shake the glorious ones with power' (Isaiah 13:13).

The mystery of Christ transforms those on earth into a new life of the gospel, as they are turned away from the older customs and from those in shadows and types who no longer have the power to prevail.

But His purpose was to arrive and proclaim, first to the Israelites, that the things lying ahead until the time of correction—that is, the law in the scriptures—will be abolished, transforming the mind of believers into a better and spiritual state.
For all things in Christ are new.

However, although they ought to obey Him, the leaders of the Jewish synagogue and the priests, who did not behave appropriately with the ornaments of holiness, resisted him in a youthful way, acting impiously and wanting to make the mystery of the economy of the Only-Begotten, which had come to them in the flesh, useless by always speaking against the law given through the all-wise Moses.
translator_notes: The text begins mid-sentence with '...to the sanctified people'.
The text ends mid-sentence with '...the mystery of the economy of the Only-Begotten'.
The clause 'Ἀπόλλωλε τοίνυν ὁμοῦ τοῖς οἰκείοις ὑπασπισταῖς, καὶ τῆς τῶν εὐσεβούντων ἀγέλης ἀπελέλακται, θηρὸς ἀνημέρου δίκην ἐπιπηδῶν·' describes the destruction of the enemy and his attendants.
The clause 'ἀνατετραμμένων δηλονότι τῶν ἀρχαιοτέρων ἐθῶν' specifies that those on earth are being turned away from older customs.

title: Uzziah's Reign and Ahaz's Apostasy
english: Uzziah was a powerful ruler who besieged and captured many cities of the Philistines, that is, the Palestinians, and from the so-called Hollow Syria.

He went out and fought against the foreigners and strengthened the walls of Gath and the walls of Azotus, and built cities in Azotus, and among the foreigners, as the Lord strengthened him against the foreigners and Arabs, who lived on the Rock, and against the Minaites (2 Chronicles 26:6-8).
The Minaites gave gifts to Uzziah, and his name was renowned as far as the entrance of Egypt, because he was strengthened as far as the upper regions.
When he died, his son Jotham succeeded him as king.
Then came Ahaz, a wicked and apostate man, who had fallen into the snares of deceit and did not do what was right in the eyes of the Lord his God, as his father David had done.

For he worshiped wood and stones, and all the host of heaven, and even passed his son through fire, sacrificing him to demons, and he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, according to the abominations of the nations whom the Lord had driven out before the children of Israel (2 Kings 16:2-4).
He also offered sacrifices on the high places and under every green tree.
The Philistines, along with the king of Syria and the king of Israel, besieged Ahaz, and he was not able to wage war against them.

Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-Pileser, the king of Assyria, saying: 'I am your servant and son; come up and save me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel who are rebelling against me' (2 Kings 16:7).
Ahaz took silver and gold found in the treasures of the house of the Lord and the house of the king and sent them as gifts to the king.
The king of Assyria heard him and came to Damascus and captured it and killed Rezin.
Uzziah, also known as Azariah, had successfully defeated the Philistines, devastating their entire land and receiving tribute and taxes from them.
Ahaz, however, hired the Assyrians and entrusted them with his affairs, and they devastated the entire land of the Philistines, leading many away as captives.
When Ahaz died, the cities of the Philistines rebelled against him, as if they had been freed from the one who oppressed them, and it was distressing…
translator_notes: The original Greek text ends with a fragment 'καὶ δυσφόρητον ὥσπε', which is translated here as 'and it was distressing…' to indicate the incomplete sentence.
The biblical quotations are from 2 Chronicles and 2 Kings, and are referenced inline with the relevant verses.

title: Redemption
english: …Not knowing the Master of all, they would not have cried out to Him.

Just as Abel's blood is said to have cried out to God, and not the blood itself having a voice, but rather the atrocity of the deed disturbing God; similarly, one might think that those who are accustomed to worshiping unclean demons might cry out in a similar way, even if they do not know the God of all.
For even if they do not know the God of all, they have been oppressed by Satan, and in some way they cry out against their oppressors, requesting help through the manner of the deed.

Thus, we say that the Egyptians cried out to God because of those who oppressed them—that is, those they had made with their own hands, and who had subjected them to a most bitter slavery, clearly the unclean demons.
But the Lord will send a man to save them.
And who is this man, but clearly Christ? That is, the only-begotten Word of God appearing in human form.
He saved not only the Egyptians, but the whole earth.
He saved by judging; and what is this judging? It is to bring a just judgment upon them.
For He handed over Satan, who had plundered them, along with the unclean demons by assuming righteous votes, to be kept in chains of darkness for the judgment of the great day.

But those whom He saved after they had undergone such unbearable oppression, He also delivered, making them His own worshipers by turning to them the light of truth and surrounding them with the garments of freedom.
Thus also the Savior says: 'Now is the judgment of this world. Now the ruler of this world will be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up, will draw all to myself' (John 12:31-34).
You see that He has judged the world, having cast out Satan, who formerly tyrannized it, and having drawn all to Himself.
For even the Egyptians have come to know Him.
And indeed, having come to know Him, they make sacrifices, they offer prayers, and they fulfill their promises.
For this is what is sung through the voice of David: 'You have vowed and will repay to the Lord our God' (Psalm 50:14).
See, then, the newness of things.

For those who formerly used to sacrifice to demons, offering their services to Satan and presenting thank offerings and fulfilling their vows—even prayers and promises—having been enlightened in their mind through Christ and illuminated by the doctrines of truth, they have fled from their ancient error.

Having come to know once for all the Creator and Lord of all, they offer to Him a service in the spirit, fulfilling pure prayers and offering sacrifices, not those through blood and the slaughter of animals.
translator_notes: The Greek text begins mid-sentence with 'ν ὅλων...', rendered as '...Not knowing...'
The Greek text ends mid-sentence with 'σφαγῆ', rendered as '...slaughter of animals.'
